claim: T cell-specific deletion of the IL-6 receptor α chain (IL-6Rα) results in impaired Th1 and Th17 T cell responses in vivo.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that T cell-specific deletion of the IL-6 receptor α chain (IL-6Rα) results in impaired Th1 and Th17 T cell responses in vivo, and a defect in Tfh function.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: T cell-specific deletion of IL-6Rα results in a defect in Tfh function.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that T cell-specific deletion of the IL-6 receptor α chain (IL-6Rα) results in impaired Th1 and Th17 T cell responses in vivo, and a defect in Tfh function.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Depletion of Tregs in IL-6RαT-KO mice rescued the Th1 but not the Th17 response.
source: Depletion of Tregs in these mice rescued the Th1 but not the Th17 response.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: IL-6 signaling in effector T cells is required to overcome Treg-mediated suppression in vivo.
source: Our data suggest that IL-6 signaling in effector T cells is required to overcome Treg-mediated suppression in vivo.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing rescue of T cell responses upon Treg depletion.

claim: IL-6 cooperates with IL-1β to block the suppressive effect of Tregs on CD4+ T cells.
source: We show that IL-6 cooperates with IL-1β to block the suppressive effect of Tregs on CD4+ T cells, at least in part by controlling their responsiveness to IL-2.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: IL-6 and IL-1β control CD4+ T cell responsiveness to IL-2 to block Treg suppression.
source: We show that IL-6 cooperates with IL-1β to block the suppressive effect of Tregs on CD4+ T cells, at least in part by controlling their responsiveness to IL-2.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing maintenance of CD25 expression in the presence of IL-6 and IL-1β.

claim: IL-6Rα-deficient T cells mount normal primary Th1 responses in the absence of Tregs.
source: In addition, although IL-6Rα-deficient T cells mount normal primary Th1 responses in the absence of Tregs, they fail to mature into functional memory cells, demonstrating a key role for IL-6 in CD4+ T cell memory formation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: IL-6Rα-deficient T cells fail to mature into functional memory cells.
source: In addition, although IL-6Rα-deficient T cells mount normal primary Th1 responses in the absence of Tregs, they fail to mature into functional memory cells, demonstrating a key role for IL-6 in CD4+ T cell memory formation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: IL-6 plays a key role in CD4+ T cell memory formation.
source: In addition, although IL-6Rα-deficient T cells mount normal primary Th1 responses in the absence of Tregs, they fail to mature into functional memory cells, demonstrating a key role for IL-6 in CD4+ T cell memory formation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing defective memory responses in IL-6RαT-KO mice.

claim: Innate immune recognition is mediated by pattern recognition receptors including TLRs, NLRs, CLRs, and RLRs.
source: Innate immune recognition is mediated by a variety of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Iwasaki and Medzhitov, 2004), NOD-like receptors (NLRs) (Martinon et al., 2009), C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) (Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009), and retinoic acid inducible gene-I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs) (Pichlmair and Reis e Sousa, 2007), all of which recognize conserved molecular structures specific to microbes (pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or PAMPs) and activate adaptive immune responses through the induction of DC maturation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors recognize conserved molecular structures specific to microbes (PAMPs).
source: Innate immune recognition is mediated by a variety of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Iwasaki and Medzhitov, 2004), NOD-like receptors (NLRs) (Martinon et al., 2009), C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) (Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009), and retinoic acid inducible gene-I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs) (Pichlmair and Reis e Sousa, 2007), all of which recognize conserved molecular structures specific to microbes (pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or PAMPs) and activate adaptive immune responses through the induction of DC maturation.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors activate adaptive immune responses through the induction of DC maturation.
source: Innate immune recognition is mediated by a variety of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) (Iwasaki and Medzhitov, 2004), NOD-like receptors (NLRs) (Martinon et al., 2009), C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) (Geijtenbeek and Gringhuis, 2009), and retinoic acid inducible gene-I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs) (Pichlmair and Reis e Sousa, 2007), all of which recognize conserved molecular structures specific to microbes (pathogen-associated molecular patterns, or PAMPs) and activate adaptive immune responses through the induction of DC maturation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and supported by citations to established literature.

claim: DC maturation involves redistribution of MHC molecules from intracellular endocytic compartments to the cell surface.
source: The DC maturation process involves a redistribution of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules from intracellular endocytic compartments to the cell surface, increased expression of costimulatory molecules, and secretion of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which is essential for the activation of naive T cells (Banchereau and Steinman, 1998).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: DC maturation involves increased expression of costimulatory molecules.
source: The DC maturation process involves a redistribution of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules from intracellular endocytic compartments to the cell surface, increased expression of costimulatory molecules, and secretion of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which is essential for the activation of naive T cells (Banchereau and Steinman, 1998).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: DC maturation involves secretion of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

claim: TLR-induced DC maturation and migration to draining lymph nodes, in the absence of TLR-induced inflammatory cytokines, is insufficient for the induction of T cell activation.

claim: T cell responses are controlled by naturally occurring CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs).
source: T cell responses are controlled by naturally occurring CD4+ CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), which play an important role in maintaining immune tolerance and homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Tregs play an important role in maintaining immune tolerance and homeostasis.

claim: The absence of Foxp3 results in the development of a fatal autoimmune disease.

claim: Cytokines produced by DCs following TLR activation are critical for releasing responder CD4+ T cells from suppression by Tregs.

claim: IL-6 was implicated as a mediator for blocking Treg suppressor activity based on in vitro experiments and analysis of complete IL-6 KO mice.

claim: The pleiotropic nature of IL-6 has made it difficult to assess the T cell-specific function of this cytokine in vivo.

claim: IL-6 has been previously described as a B cell growth factor.

claim: IL-6 has been previously described as an initiator of acute phase responses.

claim: IL-6 is an important cytokine that governs the differentiation of Th17 cells.

claim: Stimulating T cells with TGF-β results in the induction of Foxp3.

claim: Combining TGF-β with IL-6 represses Foxp3 expression and induces ROR-γt, resulting in the differentiation of Th17 cells.
source: Stimulating T cells with TGF-β results in the induction of Foxp3, whereas combining TGF-β with IL-6 represses Foxp3 expression and induces retinoid-related orphan receptor (ROR)-γt, resulting in the differentiation of Th17 cells (Ivanov et al., 2006).

claim: IL-6 has been suggested to be essential for the differentiation of the T follicular helper (Tfh) cell lineage.
source: IL-6 has also been suggested to be essential for the differentiation of the T follicular helper (Tfh) cell lineage, which is defined by expression of the markers CXCR5 and programmed death receptor-1 (PD-1).

claim: Tfh cells are defined by expression of the markers CXCR5 and PD-1.

claim: The IL-6 receptor complex consists of the ligand-binding subunit IL-6Rα chain and the signal-transducing subunit gp130.
source: The IL-6 receptor complex consists of the ligand-binding subunit, the IL-6Rα chain, and the signal-transducing subunit, gp130 (Taga et al., 1989), which is a common signaling transducer for several cytokines including IL-6, IL-11, leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), oncostatin M (OSM), cardiotrophin-1 (CT-1), and IL-35.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: gp130 is a common signaling transducer for several cytokines including IL-6, IL-11, LIF, OSM, CT-1, and IL-35.
source: The IL-6 receptor complex consists of the ligand-binding subunit, the IL-6Rα chain, and the signal-transducing subunit, gp130 (Taga et al., 1989), which is a common signaling transducer for several cytokines including IL-6, IL-11, leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), oncostatin M (OSM), cardiotrophin-1 (CT-1), and IL-35.

claim: Homodimerization of gp130 upon IL-6 binding results in the subsequent phosphorylation of the transcription factors STAT1 and STAT3.
source: Homodimerization of gp130 upon IL-6 binding results in the activation of the gp130-associated tyrosine kinases JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 and the subsequent phosphorylation of the transcription factors STAT1 and STAT3 (Kamimura et al., 2003).

claim: The soluble form of the IL-6Rα chain is capable of binding to IL-6 and activating cells through association with gp130.
source: In addition to the membrane-bound receptor, a soluble form of the IL-6Rα chain can be generated through either alternative splicing or proteolytic cleavage and is capable of binding to IL-6 and activating cells through association with gp130 (Kamimura et al., 2003).

claim: Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the periphery of IL-6RαT-KO mice failed to express the IL-6Rα.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from IL-6RαT-KO mice remained deficient of the IL-6Rα after immunization with OVA and LPS in IFA.
source: Importantly, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from IL-6RαT-KO mice remained deficient of the IL-6Rα after immunization with Ovalbumin (OVA) and LPS emulsified in Incomplete Freund's Adjuvant (IFA) as a carrier, suggesting that the release of the soluble form of the IL-6Rα during the immune response does not restore IL-6 signaling in these cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The release of the soluble form of the IL-6Rα during the immune response does not restore IL-6 signaling in IL-6RαT-KO T cells.
source: Importantly, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from IL-6RαT-KO mice remained deficient of the IL-6Rα after immunization with Ovalbumin (OVA) and LPS emulsified in Incomplete Freund's Adjuvant (IFA) as a carrier, suggesting that the release of the soluble form of the IL-6Rα during the immune response does not restore IL-6 signaling in these cells (Figure 1A).

claim: IL-6-induced STAT3 phosphorylation was blocked in IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ and CD8+ T cells compared to control wild-type T cells.

claim: Addition of IL-6 to CD4+ T cells phosphorylated STAT3 very effectively in WT cells but not in IL-6Rα-deficient cells.

evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of the soluble form of the IL-6Rα together with IL-6 rescued the phosphorylation of STAT3 in IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells.

evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: IL-11, OSM, or CNTF did not phosphorylate STAT3 in either wild-type or IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells.
source: Importantly, the addition of the soluble form of the IL-6Rα (sIL6Rα) together with IL-6 rescued the phosphorylation of STAT3 in IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells whereas IL-11, OSM, or CNTF did not phosphorylate STAT3 in either wild-type or IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The STAT3-dependent signaling pathway remains intact in IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells.

claim: Other tested cytokines of the IL-6 family do not play a major role in the activation of naive CD4+ T cells.
source: These results suggest that the STAT3-dependent signaling pathway remains intact in IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells and that other tested cytokines of the IL-6 family do not play a major role in the activation of naive CD4+ T cells.

claim: T cells isolated from IL-6RαT-KO mice showed impaired proliferation upon restimulation with antigen.

evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by [3H]-thymidine incorporation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD4+ T cells from IL-6RαT-KO mice failed to produce IL-17.

claim: IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ CD45RBhi T cells failed to induce colitis when transferred into RAG2 KO mice.

claim: The Th17 response of IL-6RαT-KO mice was defective.

claim: Immunization of IL-6RαT-KO mice with OVA and LPS in IFA revealed a profound defect in the Th1 response.

claim: IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to secrete robust amounts of IFN-γ after restimulation with antigen.
source: However, immunization of the IL-6RαT-KO mice with OVA and LPS in IFA also revealed a profound defect in the Th1 response as IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to secrete robust amounts of IFN-γ after restimulation with antigen (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Similar results were obtained following immunization with OVA and other TLR ligands such as PGN, CpG DNA, or CFA.

claim: T cells from IL-6RαT-KO mice were impaired in their ability to proliferate following restimulation.

claim: IL-6RαT-KO T cells remained deficient in IL-17, regardless of proliferation.

claim: The defect in the IFN-γ response is not due to a requirement for IL-6 in the differentiation of IFN-γ-producing cells.

claim: The IFN-γ response is deficient in IL-6RαT-KO mice as a consequence of impaired T cell proliferation.

claim: There was no difference in cell death between WT and IL-6Rα-deficient CD4+ T cells on day 7 following immunization.

claim: IL-6 signaling plays a role in regulating T cell expansion and the subsequent induction of Th1 responses in vivo.
